To reduce operation within a rotation-prohibited frequency range and prevent resonance in a gas compressor controlled by an inverter, the gas compressor includes: a compressor main body that compresses gas; a motor that rotationally drives the compressor main body; an inverter that varies the rotational speed of the motor; a check valve disposed downstream of the compressor main body; pressure detection means that detects load-side pressure downstream of the check valve; and a control device that controls the frequency output by the inverter in accordance with the pressure detected by the pressure detection means.

The control device performs control such that compressed gas having a prescribed pressure is generated and maintained by increasing or decreasing the frequency. When the frequency required to generate the compressed gas having the prescribed pressure includes a specific frequency, the output frequency of the inverter is increased or decreased when the pressure detected by the pressure detection means reaches a pressure corresponding to a frequency that has a pressure width more constant than the prescribed pressure and does not include the specific frequency.

The controller raises or lowers the frequency so that compressed gas at a predetermined pressure is produced and maintained. The gas compressor is designed to maintain stable compressed gas pressure while avoiding operation at motor speeds that may cause resonance or other undesirable vibration. To achieve this, the compressor uses inverter control to adjust the rotational speed of the motor. By changing the inverter output frequency, the system can increase or decrease the operating speed of the compressor as needed, while reducing or preventing operation within rotation-prohibited frequency ranges.

The compressor includes several main components: a compressor body that compresses the gas, a motor that drives the compressor body, an inverter that controls the motor speed, a check valve provided downstream of the compressor to prevent reverse flow, a pressure detector that detects the pressure of the compressed gas downstream of the compressor, and a control device that manages the operation of the inverter.

During operation, the control device monitors the downstream compressed gas pressure detected by the pressure detector. Based on this detected pressure, the control device adjusts the inverter output frequency to control the motor speed. If the detected pressure is lower than the prescribed target pressure, the control device increases the inverter output frequency to raise the motor speed and increase the compressor output. If the detected pressure is higher than the prescribed target pressure, the control device decreases the inverter output frequency to lower the motor speed and reduce the compressor output. In this way, the compressor maintains the compressed gas pressure within a prescribed range.

However, certain inverter output frequencies may correspond to rotational speeds at which resonance is likely to occur in the compressor, motor, piping, frame, or other related components. These resonance-prone frequencies are treated as specific prohibited frequencies or prohibited frequency ranges. When the frequency required to maintain the prescribed compressed gas pressure would include such a specific prohibited frequency, the control device does not simply command operation at that frequency. Instead, it shifts the inverter output frequency away from the resonance-prone frequency.

The frequency adjustment is performed on the basis of the detected downstream pressure. Rather than allowing the inverter output frequency to pass through or remain at the specific prohibited frequency, the control device selects a frequency on either the higher-frequency side or the lower-frequency side of the prohibited range. The selected frequency is determined so that the downstream compressed gas pressure remains within an allowable target pressure range while avoiding the prohibited frequency. As a result, the compressor can continue to supply compressed gas at an appropriate pressure without operating continuously in a frequency range that may cause resonance or excessive vibration.

This control method enables both pressure stability and mechanical reliability. By coordinating pressure feedback control with frequency avoidance control, the gas compressor can maintain the required compressed gas pressure while reducing the risk of vibration, noise, component fatigue, or damage caused by operation at resonance-prone rotational speeds.
outputs.L4:
A gas compressor is provided with a drive motor whose rotational speed is controlled by an inverter, so that the discharge capacity of the compressor can be varied according to demand. In operation, certain motor or compressor rotation-frequency ranges may coincide with mechanical resonance regions of the compressor body, piping, mounting structure, or other connected components. Continuous operation in such resonance-prone ranges can increase vibration and noise and may reduce reliability. To address this, the compressor system is configured to avoid, or reduce the amount of time spent in, predetermined prohibited rotation-frequency ranges.

The compressor includes a pressure detector arranged downstream of the compressor, for example in a discharge line, receiver tank, or compressed-gas supply passage. The pressure detector detects the pressure of the compressed gas delivered by the compressor. A controller receives the detected pressure and controls the output frequency of the inverter, thereby controlling the rotational speed of the motor and the discharge amount of the compressor. Under ordinary conditions, the controller adjusts the inverter output frequency so that the downstream compressed-gas pressure is maintained within a prescribed pressure range or near a target pressure.

The controller stores information identifying at least one prohibited rotation frequency, or prohibited rotation-frequency range, in which operation of the compressor should be avoided because of resonance. The controller also stores or calculates a relationship between the compressed-gas pressure, the required compressor capacity, and the inverter frequency needed to maintain that pressure. When the frequency required for normal pressure control does not fall within a prohibited range, the controller performs normal inverter control and maintains the compressed-gas pressure within the prescribed pressure band.

However, when the inverter frequency required to maintain the prescribed compressed-gas pressure would include, pass through, or remain near a specific prohibited frequency, the controller modifies the control operation. In such a case, the controller shifts the inverter output frequency away from the prohibited frequency at a corresponding pressure point. Instead of controlling the compressor precisely around the resonance-prone frequency, the controller selects a nearby allowable frequency above or below the prohibited range. At the same time, the controller applies a wider stable pressure band associated with that shifted frequency, so that the compressed-gas pressure can still be maintained within an acceptable range without requiring operation at the prohibited frequency.

For example, if the detected downstream pressure indicates that the compressor would ordinarily be driven at a frequency falling within a prohibited resonance range, the controller may increase the inverter frequency to a value above the prohibited range until the pressure reaches an upper limit of the widened pressure band. The controller may then reduce or suspend capacity, or shift to a lower allowable frequency below the prohibited range, until the pressure approaches a lower limit of the widened pressure band. Conversely, the controller may select a lower allowable frequency when appropriate, depending on the pressure state and the required compressed-gas supply. By permitting pressure variation within the wider stable band, the system avoids repeated or continuous operation at the prohibited frequency while still supplying compressed gas at a usable pressure.

Thus, the compressor system maintains the downstream compressed-gas pressure by inverter control while preventing the motor and compressor from operating in resonance-prone rotation-frequency ranges. This reduces vibration and noise, improves durability of the compressor and connected equipment, and enables stable compressed-gas supply without requiring additional mechanical damping devices or complex structural modifications.

**The Power of “The”**

The word **“the”** may seem small, but it is one of the most important words in the English language. It is called a **definite article**, and it is used when we are talking about something specific. For example, “a book” can mean any book, but “the book” means a particular book that the speaker and listener both understand.

“The” helps make sentences clearer. It points to people, places, objects, or ideas that are already known or unique. We say **“the sun”** because there is only one sun in our sky, and **“the teacher”** when we mean a specific teacher. Without “the,” many sentences would feel incomplete or unclear.

Although it is only three letters long, “the” plays a big role in communication. It gives meaning, focus, and precision to English sentences. This simple word shows that even the smallest parts of language can be powerful.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a single-paragraph patent abstract describing a gas compressor with a motor, inverter, downstream check valve, pressure sensor, and controller that avoids operation in a prohibited resonant frequency range while maintaining prescribed compressed-gas pressure.
counterfactuals.output: A gas compressor system includes a compression mechanism driven by an electric motor, an inverter configured to supply variable-frequency power to the motor, a check valve disposed downstream of the compression mechanism to prevent reverse flow of compressed gas, a pressure sensor configured to detect a pressure of the compressed gas downstream of the compression mechanism, and a controller coupled to the inverter and the pressure sensor. The controller controls an operating frequency or rotational speed of the motor to maintain the detected pressure at or near a prescribed target pressure, while inhibiting operation of the motor within a predetermined prohibited frequency range corresponding to a resonant frequency range of the compressor system. When pressure control would otherwise require operation within the prohibited range, the controller selects an allowable operating frequency above or below the prohibited range and adjusts the inverter output accordingly, thereby suppressing vibration or noise due to resonance while continuing to supply compressed gas at the prescribed pressure.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an English patent-style summary for an invention where an inverter-controlled compressor adjusts motor frequency based on downstream pressure and shifts frequency when the pressure-maintaining frequency includes a specific resonance frequency.
counterfactuals.output:
An inverter-controlled compressor system is provided in which a compressor motor is driven at a variable operating frequency determined in accordance with a detected downstream pressure of compressed fluid. A controller receives a pressure signal from a pressure sensor disposed on a discharge side of the compressor and determines a pressure-maintaining frequency required to maintain the downstream pressure at or near a target pressure.

When the determined pressure-maintaining frequency falls within, coincides with, or otherwise includes a predetermined resonance frequency range associated with the compressor, motor, piping, mounting structure, or another component of the system, the controller shifts the operating frequency away from the resonance frequency. The shifted frequency may be set to a higher or lower non-resonant frequency while maintaining the downstream pressure within an allowable pressure range. In some embodiments, the controller alternates between adjacent non-resonant frequencies, applies a correction offset, or modifies the target frequency according to a stored resonance avoidance map.

By avoiding continuous operation at the resonance frequency while still controlling discharge pressure, the compressor system suppresses vibration, reduces noise, prevents mechanical fatigue, and improves durability without requiring additional mechanical damping components. The invention is particularly applicable to variable-speed air compressors and other fluid compression systems in which pressure control and resonance avoidance are both required.

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a technical patent abstract explaining how a gas compressor prevents resonance by increasing or decreasing inverter output frequency when the pressure corresponding to a target-pressure frequency includes a specific frequency, using load-side pressure feedback.
counterfactuals.output: A gas compressor system includes a compressor driven by an electric motor, an inverter configured to supply variable-frequency power to the motor, a pressure sensor disposed on a load side of the compressor, and a controller. The controller determines, from load-side pressure feedback, a target-pressure frequency corresponding to an operating frequency required to achieve or maintain a target discharge pressure. When the target-pressure frequency includes, coincides with, or falls within a predetermined specific frequency or resonance frequency range associated with vibration or acoustic resonance of the compressor system, piping, or connected load, the controller prevents continuous operation at the specific frequency by correcting the inverter output frequency upward or downward to a non-resonant frequency. The correction may be selected based on pressure deviation, operating state, or a predefined avoidance band, such that the compressor output pressure remains within an allowable range while resonance is suppressed. By using load-side pressure feedback to identify the pressure-correlated operating frequency and selectively increasing or decreasing the inverter output frequency away from the specific frequency, the system reduces vibration, noise, and mechanical stress without requiring additional damping structures.
